definition.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion and the loss of fertility from overuse, acidification, salinization or contamination.

facts.text: Deforestation typically causes large-scale erosion, nutrient loss and sometimes desertification.
Techniques include crop rotation, cover crops, conservation tillage and windbreaks.
Farmers have practised it for millennia.
The EU's Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, winter cover crops, plant residues and grass margins.
Solving erosion also needs political and economic action, including changing how land is valued.
Each one percent increase in soil organic matter lets soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre.
Taxing pesticides at different rates is one option studied for cutting their use.

definition.text: Ploughing furrows along a slope's contour lines so they stay level, which slows runoff.

facts.text: It can raise crop yields by 10 to 50 percent, partly by keeping soil in place.
The ancient Phoenicians used it on slopes of two to ten percent.

definition.text: Cutting a hillside into a series of nearly level steps for growing crops.

facts.text: Terraces slow the rapid runoff of irrigation water and are more common on small farms.

definition.text: An extension of contour farming that shapes contour lines around the whole watershed.

facts.text: It is used in regenerative farms alongside diverse livestock and crop production.

definition.text: Preventing and reducing the build-up of salt in soil, which mainly comes from irrigating with salty water.

facts.text: Salt breaks down soil structure and causes infertility; salinity affects about one third of the earth's arable land.
After the 1970 Aswan Dam, a raised water table salinised soils in Egypt.
Salt-tolerant plants such as saltbush can lower water tables and slow surface salt build-up.

title: Soil health

definition.text: The state of a soil that performs the full range of ecosystem functions suited to its environment.

facts.text: It arises from good interactions among a soil's living and non-living parts, such as microbes, plants and animals.
It covers sustaining productivity, biodiversity, water and air quality, and human health.
The term has largely replaced soil quality, which judged soil only for one purpose such as growing maize.
It depends on soil biodiversity and improves when soil is kept covered and given carbon-rich amendments.
Some microbiologists believe 80% of soil nutrient functions are controlled by microbes.
US soils have lost up to 75% of their carbon over 40 years, though how much is debated.
A soil can be healthy for ecosystems without directly serving crop production, so terms and measures are debated.

contested_note: Scientists debate how to define and measure soil health, since ecological and agronomic goals can conflict.

definition.text: Measuring a soil's physical, chemical and biological condition against benchmarks of healthy function.

facts.text: Benchmarks include CO2 release, humus levels, microbial activity and available calcium.
Many labs resist new biological tests because fertility testing rests on crop-response models with no equivalent for soil health.
